The method originates from the application of continuum mechanics concepts, specifically the Reynolds transport theorem for evolving surfaces, to differentiable rendering [S2, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in Section 3.3 that the transport relation used for differentiating surface integrals in differentiable rendering 'originated in fluid mechanics [Cermelli et al. 2005]' and is based on 'concepts described in §3.2'. Section 3.2 details the application of continuum mechanics concepts, specifically defining evolving surfaces, material/spatial fields, and deriving the derivative of integrals over these surfaces (Eq. 11), which is identified as the Reynolds transport relation. The claim accurately reflects that the method applies these continuum mechanics concepts (specifically the Reynolds transport theorem for evolving surfaces) to differentiable rendering.

The claim states that the evidence supports the use of rendering integrals over implicit surfaces that evolve with parameters, especially when discontinuities are present. Source [S1] explicitly discusses 'differentiable rendering of evolving closed implicit surfaces' and the differentiation of path integrals. Source [S2] provides the mathematical framework for differentiating surface integrals over evolving surfaces, specifically addressing 'discontinuity curves' and deriving a transport relation that includes boundary terms for these discontinuities. Both sources confirm the context of differentiating rendering integrals over evolving implicit surfaces with discontinuities.

*   **Implicit Mapping Limitations**: Defining a global one-to-one mapping $X(\cdot, \pi)$ for all $\pi$ for implicit surfaces is hard or impossible; the method often relies on local parameterizations or the specific normal-offset approximation $X(\mathbf{p}, \pi) = \mathbf{p} + t(\mathbf{p}, \pi)\mathbf{n}_B(\mathbf{p})$ which is only one-to-one at $\pi=0$ [S1].

The claim accurately reflects the content of Source [S1]. The source explicitly states that 'it is hard—if not impossible—to define a one-to-one mapping X(·, 𝜋) that transforms the reference surface B to the evolving M (𝜋) for all 𝜋.' It further specifies that the method uses the mapping X(𝒑, 𝜋) := 𝒑 + 𝑡 (𝒑, 𝜋) 𝒏 B (𝒑) and notes that this mapping is 'only one-to-one at 𝜋 = 0.' All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
